title: How Hurricanes Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how hurricanes form and what they become. They open with a book plug and Bob Dylan banter, then cover the basics: hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are the same storm under different regional names; the Atlantic season runs roughly June 1 to November. Formation requires warm ocean water (about 80 F down to roughly 150 feet), rising moist air, converging winds, low wind shear, and the Coriolis effect, which sets rotation direction and keeps the eye clear. They walk through Saffir-Simpson style categories by wind speed, the damage each category causes, and building codes and stilt houses after Hurricane Andrew. They discuss storm surge, Hurricane Harvey's costs and wildlife impacts, and forecasting (satellites, spaghetti models, and the Cone of Uncertainty). They cover the history of hurricane naming (saints' days, then male and female names, the WMO lists, retired names), a myth about women's names, and historical storms including the 1274 Mongol fleet sunk off Japan (kamikaze). They close with climate change and its effect on storm frequency and intensity, the 2020 season outlook, and a listener email about conservatism and anti-monopoly laws.

segments.title: Book plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh plugs the forthcoming Stuff You Should Know book and its preorder gift. The hosts banter about Bob Dylan songs and introduce the hurricane topic.

segments.title: Hurricanes, typhoons, and cyclones
segments.summary: The hosts explain that hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are the same kind of storm, named by region. They cover the seasons in the Northern and Southern hemispheres, where each type forms, and the origin of the word hurricane from a Mayan god.

segments.title: Where hurricanes form and how they weaken
segments.summary: Overview of conditions that favor hurricane formation: warm ocean water near the equator and tropics, rising moist air, and the typical west-to-east track from Africa across the Atlantic. Storms weaken on landfall or when they move over cooler water.

segments.title: The science of hurricane formation
segments.summary: Explains the chain of events from warm sea surface (at least 80 F down to about 150 feet) to rising, condensing moist air, converging surface winds, the latent heat of condensation, and the need for low wind shear. Thunderstorms organize into a tropical depression and then a storm.

segments.title: Coriolis effect and the eye of the hurricane
segments.summary: The Coriolis effect makes hurricanes rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. It also deflects winds so they never reach the low-pressure center, creating the calm eye. The hosts note the effect is weakest at the equator.

segments.title: Hurricane categories and damage
segments.summary: Describes the Saffir-Simpson style categories by wind speed, with typical damage at each level from category one through five, and the power and water outages that follow.

segments.title: Building codes, storm surge, and Hurricane Harvey
segments.summary: Discusses coastal housing, stilts, and building codes after Hurricane Andrew. Explains roof failure from pressure differences and storm surge that pushes ocean inland and reshapes coastlines. Describes Hurricane Harvey's costs and impacts on sewers, drinking water, and wildlife.

segments.title: Hurricane tracking, forecasting, and the Cone of Uncertainty
segments.summary: Covers satellite and infrared tracking by regional meteorological centers, the spaghetti model, and the European model. Explains that the Cone of Uncertainty shows the possible track of the storm's center over forecast periods, not its size.

segments.title: Hurricane names, history, and myths
segments.summary: Traces naming from Catholic saints' days in the West Indies to military alphabet names in World War II, then male and female names alternating after feminist objections. Lists the 2020 Atlantic names and the separate naming lists for other regions. Discusses retired names and a debunked myth that women's names are deadlier.

segments.title: Historical hurricanes and the Mongol fleet
segments.summary: Notes that hurricanes have always occurred, with evidence from cave drawings and lake-bed studies. Recounts the 1274 storm that sank the Mongol invasion fleet off Japan, which gave rise to the name kamikaze.

segments.title: Climate change and the 2020 season
segments.summary: Reports that Category 4 and 5 storms have roughly doubled since the 1970s, and explains why warmer oceans may fuel stronger storms while open questions remain about ocean heating depth. Mentions the early 2020 storms, La Nina, and Saharan dust as factors for that season.

segments.title: Listener mail: conservatism and anti-monopoly laws
segments.summary: A listener named Tim from Minnesota writes about the Robber Barons episode, explaining a conservative view of limited government and support for anti-monopoly laws. The hosts thank him.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and contact information for the show.
